UX case study, self initiated, not affiliated with PharmEasy

Where PharmEasy's Checkout Breaks Trust

PharmEasy is one of India's largest online pharmacies. I set out to buy Dolo 650 for a fever and hit five separate breakdowns before I could pay for it, starting with wrong-name substitutes in search and ending with an address form that has no field for the one thing its own error message demands. This documents all five with real evidence, then redesigns each one.

Project summary
RoleUX Researcher & Product Designer
DurationSeptember 2026, ongoing
TeamIndependent redesign, solo, no team
PlatformPharmEasy's web checkout, pharmeasy.in
ResponsibilitiesAudit, five user interviews, synthesis, redesign, prototyping notes
StatusSelf initiated redesign concept. Not live, not commissioned, not affiliated with PharmEasy.
The headline problem: this isn't only about clarity or trust. As of this audit, a first-time guest cannot complete checkout at all, the address form has no field to enter a name, but won't let you continue without one. Everything else in this case study is real too, but this one stops the task cold.

3

Problem & Goals

DONE

Problem statement

A shopper needs to search for, price, and pay for a real medicine on PharmEasy. At nearly every stage, from the search result to the final address field, the interface shows something that isn't true or is missing something it requires, and at the very last stage, it's missing the one thing it demands: a field to enter a name, without which the order cannot be placed at all.

Design goals

  • Label substitute brands clearly, distinct from the exact medicine searched for.
  • Match the price shown before login to the price charged after.
  • Disclose delivery fee, platform fee, and order minimum before a cart exists.
  • Default every substitution to the item actually searched for.
  • Never require a field the form doesn't provide, starting with Name on the address step.
BeforeAfter
Unlabeled substitutes mixed into search resultsExact match and alternates clearly tagged
Guest price doesn't match the price chargedOne real price, guest or signed in
Fees and minimum order hidden until after loginDisclosed on the product page, before a cart exists
Substitution pre-selects a different manufacturerSearched item stays selected by default
Address form has no Name field, checkout is blockedName field added, order can be placed

Research & Diagnosis

DONE
MethodFindingDesign implication
Live walkthrough & heuristic reviewSearch, pricing, substitution, and address entry each broke a different Nielsen heuristicDocumented as eight real exhibits; every redesign below ties back to one
Form audit, address stepThe form's own validation error references a "Name" field the form never rendersFlagged as the highest-severity fix, this alone blocks every order
Competitive review (1mg)A direct competitor already discloses fees up front and never pre-selects a substituteConfirmed the pricing and substitution fixes are realistic, not idealistic
User interviews (5)Every interviewee wanted an active choice on substitution; assisted shoppers can't independently verify a price changeHardened "default to the searched item" as non-negotiable, not just a nice-to-have

The five interviews, a price-conscious student, a convenience-focused professional, a caretaker ordering for a parent, a small-business owner whose son orders for him, and a retiree who relies on her daughter, covered recall questions on pricing and substitution, plus a live reaction to the real screenshots above. Notes were cleaned up with an AI tool for clarity, closely enough that some exact wording may not match the original conversations word for word, but the substance reflects what was actually said. None of them hit the address-form bug directly, since that surfaced later in a follow-up pass, but it's the same pattern the interviews already confirmed people don't forgive: a form that doesn't do what it claims to.

6

Design Decisions

DONE

1. Label substitutes at the moment of search

Before

Leemol, Dolopar, and Calpol 650 appear in search results styled identically to Dolo 650, the exact match. Nothing distinguishes them.

Design change

Tag the exact match "Exact match" and every alternate "Alternate brand, same salt," both visible at a glance, before a tap is needed.

Why

A shopper shouldn't have to already know these are substitutes to notice that they are.

2. Show the real price, and the real condition, before login

Before

A guest sees ₹24.21, 25% OFF. The cart shows ₹29.05. Logging in reveals ₹190.05, a ₹149 delivery fee and ₹12 platform fee that never appeared as a guest, and a ₹1,000-order condition on the discount disclosed only in small grey text five lines down.

Design change

Disclose delivery fee and minimum order on the product page itself, before a cart exists. Keep the 25% OFF hook exactly where it is, but move its condition to directly under the price, in the same glance, not five lines later.

Why

The number a shopper sees has to be the number they pay, from the first moment they see a price, not two steps and a login later.

Evidence

1mg, a direct competitor, already states delivery and handling charges will be "clearly disclosed before purchase," right under its own Add button. This isn't an idealistic ask.

3. Default every substitution to what was searched for

Before

The comparison drawer pre-selects Teplota 650, a different manufacturer, while Dolo 650, the medicine actually searched for, sits under a plain, unselected button.

Design change

The searched item stays selected by default, always. Switching to the alternate takes an explicit tap.

Why

Confirmed directly in interviews: every single person wanted an active choice on substitution, no exceptions, including the person most open to a cheaper alternative.

Evidence

The same pattern is already live on 1mg, which labels the searched item "Currently viewing" and pre-selects neither option.

4. Add the missing Name field to the address form

Before

The Select Address form asks for Deliver to, Mobile Number, Pincode, House number and building, Street Name, and Address Type. No field for a name, anywhere. Save and Continue is blocked by "Name must contain at least 1 letter...", a field the form never renders.

Design change

Add a required Name field, first in the form, above Deliver to.

Why

This isn't a polish issue, it's a hard stop. No amount of correct data in the other six fields lets the order through. It's the highest-severity fix in this entire case study, because it's the only one that isn't a trust problem, it's a task-completion problem.

Show the After

DRAFT
Draft redesign, not yet validated. Coded mockups and Figma screens built to test the decisions above, not final, tested screens. Each one is tied to a specific exhibit above, in the same order.

1. Search: exact match and alternates, clearly tagged

Redesign concept, search results. Not a real PharmEasy screenshot.
Dolo 650mg Strip Of 15 Tablets
15 Tablet(s) in Strip
Exact match
Leemol 650mg Strip Of 15 Tablets
15 Tablet(s) in Strip

Dolopar 650mg Strip Of 15 Tablets
15 Tablet(s) in Strip
Alternate brand, same salt

Decision 1: the exact match is tagged, not just first in the list. Alternates say plainly what they are, before a tap.

2. The full cart page: fee, minimum, and discount condition, in one real screen

After, the redesign, as a guest, before login, designed in Figma
1 2

Notice "Hello, Log in" still sitting in the top right, this is a guest, not a signed-in account, and every number on the page is already real: ₹190.05 as the total, the delivery fee, the platform fee, the ₹199 minimum. That's the actual fix behind Decision 2. It's not that the numbers changed, it's that they stopped changing depending on who's looking.

1: the substitution banner, unchanged, still honest, still optional. 2: Minimum Order (product MRP): ₹199, now a line item inside the Bill Summary. It didn't start there. An earlier draft of this redesign sat that box above the substitution banner, its own separate callout, competing for attention with everything else on the page. Moving it down, into the bill itself, put it where a shopper is actually looking when they check what they owe, one line among the numbers, not another banner shouting over the last one.

3. Substitution: the searched item stays chosen

Redesigned, designed in Figma

Decision 3: Dolo 650, the item actually searched for, stays "Selected." Switching to Teplota takes an active tap, not an uncheck on the thing already chosen.

4. Address form: a field for the name it already asks for

Redesigned, designed in Figma

Decision 4: one new field, first in the form, above Deliver to. Every other field is untouched. "Save and Continue" now has something to validate against.

None of these four fixes touch a headline, a hero image, or a single word of marketing copy. A tag on a search result. A box moved eight rows down. A default flipped. One field added to a form that already had six. Small enough that a stakeholder review could wave any one of them through without a second look, and easy to miss exactly why that's the risk: a shopper doesn't file a complaint about a missing Name field. They close the tab, open 1mg, and buy the same strip of tablets there instead. Small changes, on the interface. Not small, on whether the order happens at all.

8

Validation & Results

DRAFT

This is a self-initiated portfolio redesign, not a live product, so there's no real conversion or completion data behind it, and I'm not going to invent any. What exists: five interviews validating the pricing and substitution problems as real pain points, and a coded redesign that hasn't been shown to anyone yet.

Next step, planned but not run: a lightweight 3 to 5 person before/after comparison, specifically testing whether people notice the labeled substitutes and the new Name field without being told what changed, since those are the two decisions this round of interviews didn't directly cover.

If it shipped, this is what I'd want to measure:

Address-step completion rate
Specifically whether guests now get past Select Address on the first try
Checkout completion
Cart to checkout rate, drop-off at the login/price-reveal step
Substitution opt-out rate
Share of users who decline a swap once accepting it takes a real choice
Support tickets
Complaints citing an inability to complete an order, delivery cost surprises, or the wrong medicine arriving

Grounded in Baymard Institute's research (cited in the audit): late-revealed costs are the top cause of cart abandonment, and forced account creation is cited by 26% of shoppers as a reason they leave. The address-step metric is new to this round, added because that bug doesn't just cost trust, it costs the order outright.

What I'd change with more time

Run the before/after comparison above before calling any of this finished, especially the Name field and the search labeling, neither one has been checked against a real user yet.
I'm a product designer, not a PharmEasy employee, and this was never commissioned by them. Once validated, I plan to send this directly to their product team, the address-form bug alone is worth flagging regardless of what happens to the rest of this case study.
